body: @matthewd asked if this was related to how in tests the records aren't truly committed but I verified in a demo application that this occurs outside of the test framework so it's not related to that.

Identified. This regression is due to changing record registration order to the transaction.

In the reproduction script, `comment.post` loads new post (since automatic inverse_of is disabled due to association having lambda), then the records in the transaction will be `[<loaded (saved) post: 1>, <destroyed post: 1>]`, and `<loaded (saved) post: 1>` wins by `records.uniq`.

We should keep the registration order to avoid any regression.
I'll create a PR to fix that.

issue.title: Should take the record's state of first action in the transaction
issue.body:
If the same id's records are saved and/or destroyed in the transaction,
commit callbackes will only run for the first enrolled record.

https://github.com/rails/rails/blob/a023e2180093ebc517a642aaf21f3c7241c67657/activerecord/lib/active_record/connection_adapters/abstract/transaction.rb#L115-L119

The regression #36132 is caused due to #35920 changed the enrollment
order that the first action's record will be enrolled to last in the
transaction.

We could not change the the enrollment order as long as someone depends
on the enrollment order.

Fixes #36132.

Probably this will also fix #36082.

body:
I believe we might have a similar issue related to associated records which attempt to delete their `belongs_to` association. In this modified version of Eileen's script, `Comment` will delete `Post` if there are no other comments remaining.

```ruby
# frozen_string_literal: true

require "active_record"
require "minitest/autorun"
require "logger"

# This connection will do for database-independent bug reports.
ActiveRecord::Base.establish_connection(adapter: "sqlite3", database: ":memory:")
ActiveRecord::Base.logger = Logger.new(STDOUT)

ActiveRecord::Schema.define do
  create_table :posts, force: true do |t|
    t.string :title
  end

  create_table :comments, force: true do |t|
    t.text :comment_body
    t.integer :post_id
  end
end

class Post < ActiveRecord::Base
  # This never gets called when order and an after_destroy
  # callback that updates Post is called
  after_commit on: :destroy do
    self.callback_called << "yes"
  end

  # If we don’t have a lamdba OR don’t have a callback on comment this passes
  has_many :comments, -> { order("comments.id DESC") }, dependent: :destroy

  def callback_called
    @callback_called ||= []
  end

  def callback_called=(callback_called)
    @callback_called = [callback_called]
  end
end

class Comment < ActiveRecord::Base
  belongs_to :post

  # Remove this and Post’s after_commit callbacks will be called.
  after_destroy :destroy_post_if_last_comment

  def destroy_post_if_last_comment
    post.destroy if post && post.comments.empty?
  end
end

class BugTest < Minitest::Test
  def test_after_commit
    post = Post.create!(title: "I am a post")
    comment = post.comments.create(comment_body: "i am a comment")

    assert_equal 1, post.comments.count

    post.destroy

    # pass - post is successfully deleted
    assert !Post.exists?(post.id)
    # pass - comments are successfully deleted
    assert_equal 0, Comment.where(post_id: post.id).count
    # fail - callbacks are not called when order, dependency, and an after_destroy
    # callback is used.
    assert_equal ["yes"], post.callback_called
  end
end
```

I don't have a whole lot of an idea about what's happening, but I did notice that multiple instances of the Post record are added to the transaction records (i.e. `self.class.connection.current_transaction.records`) and saw this in `ActiveRecord::Persistence#destroy`:

```
@_trigger_destroy_callback = if persisted?
  destroy_row > 0
else
  true
end
```

It seems as though the original Post record is registered, then a second Post instance for the same `id` is created via the `Comment` after destroy callback. The second `Post` instance is destroyed first. When the first `Post` instance later calls `destroy_row` there is no database record to destroy so `@_trigger_destroy_callback` is set to false. Because this first registered record is the one we check for callbacks, and `@_trigger_destroy_callback` on that record is not true the callbacks do not run.

cc/ @eileencodes @kamipo for guidance
cc/  @jhawthorn @tenderlove for visibility
